desc: Trace direct reclaim events. Uses Linux eBPF/bcc.
r: drsnoop - Trace direct reclaim events. Uses Linux eBPF/bcc.

drsnoop trace direct reclaim events, showing which processes are allocing pages with direct reclaiming. This can be useful for discovering when allocstall (/p- roc/vmstat) continues to increase, whether it is caused by some critical proc- esses or not.

This works by tracing the direct reclaim events using kernel tracepoints.

This makes use of a Linux 4.4 feature (bpf_perf_event_output()); for kernels older than 4.4, see the version under tools/old, which uses an older mechanism.

Since this uses BPF, only the root user can use this tool.

<dl><dt data-o="">-h</dt><dd>Print usage message.</dd><dt data-o="">-T</dt><dd>Include a timestamp column.</dd><dt data-o="">-U</dt><dd>Show UID.</dd><dt data-o="">-p PID</dt><dd>Trace this process ID only (filtered in-kernel).</dd><dt data-o="">-t TID</dt><dd>Trace this thread ID only (filtered in-kernel).</dd><dt data-o="">-u UID</dt><dd>Trace this UID only (filtered in-kernel).</dd><dt data-o="">-d DURATION</dt><dd>Total duration of trace in seconds.</dd><dt data-o="">-n name</dt><dd>Only print processes where its name partially matches 'name' -v verbose Run in verbose mode. Will output system memory state</dd><dt data-o="">-v</dt><dd>show system memory state</dd></dl>

Trace all direct reclaim events:
# drsnoop
Trace all direct reclaim events, for 10 seconds only:
# drsnoop -d 10
Trace all direct reclaim events, and include timestamps:
# drsnoop -T
Show UID:
# drsnoop -U
Trace PID 181 only:
# drsnoop -p 181
Trace UID 1000 only:
# drsnoop -u 1000
Trace all direct reclaim events from processes where its name partially match-
es 'mond': # drnsnoop -n mond
<dl><dt>TIME(s)</dt><dd>Time of the call, in seconds.</dd><dt>UID</dt><dd>User ID</dd><dt>PID</dt><dd>Process ID</dd><dt>TID</dt><dd>Thread ID</dd><dt>COMM</dt><dd>Process name</dd></dl>
This traces the kernel direct reclaim tracepoints and prints output for each event. As the rate of this is generally expected to be low (< 1000/s), the overhead is also expected to be negligible.

This is from bcc.

https://github.com/iovisor/bcc

Also look in the bcc distribution for a companion _examples.txt file containing example usage, output, and commentary for this tool.
